title: Fragment of a pediment from Maʾrib with a nude fertility goddess in vine leaves and grapes — the Walters Art Museum names Greco-Roman influence in South Arabia in its own words
language_note: Museum catalogue record in English. The object carries no inscription the Walters transcribes and this record claims no source-language text. On a find record `original_text_excerpt` holds the institution's object description and nothing else.
date: 2nd century CE (Sabaean), as the Walters dates it — and the description dates the STYLE separately, to "the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE", which is the sentence the record exists for.
findspot: NOT RECORDED. The Walters states a place of ORIGIN and no findspot: its `GEOGRAPHIES` field reads `Yemen, Marib (Place of Origin)`. The provenance chain is market-derived and the museum publishes it in full — `James Nash, London, 1963, by purchase; Giraud and Carolyn Foster, Baltimore, 1965, by purchase; Walters Art Museum, 2014, by gift.` The object was exhibited in 2008 as `Faces of Ancient Arabia: The Giraud and Carolyn Foster Collection of South Arabian Art`. All of that is the museum's, quoted rather than summarised, because a South Arabian object with a London-market provenance is one whose chain a later reader will want to see rather than be told about.

origin_places.name: Maʾrib (Marib), Yemen — the Walters' stated place of origin
origin_places.note:
`stated` because the museum's own `GEOGRAPHIES` field names it — `Yemen, Marib (Place of Origin)` — which is the same footing on which `africa-02-aksumite-coin` takes Aksum from a British Museum field. THE ID WAS RE-CHECKED IN THIS SESSION AND NOT INHERITED FROM `arabia-07-cih541`, which took it yesterday. `--find "Mariaba"` against the pinned 2026-08-10 snapshot returns `no place title or description matches` and one attested name, `39379 'Μαρίαβα' (Mariaba)` — which is why `--names-dump` exists and why searching for `Maʾrib` finds nothing. Entry 39379 was then read out of `data/gazetteer.json`: title `Mari(a)ba`, description `Capital of the Sabaean kingdom.`, repr_point 45.336/15.427, `location_precision` `precise`, feature types `ruin, settlement, tell`. Confirmed on the description and the coordinate before being taken, because a name match is not an identification.

THE SAME PLACE AS `arabia-07-cih541`, AND A DIFFERENT BLOCK. There the town is the FINDSPOT of a dam inscription and the excerpt's own line 81 names it; here it is the place of MANUFACTURE of an object whose findspot nobody recorded. The two blocks exist so that one place can hold two relations without the map claiming they are the same claim.

original_text_excerpt: The upper left side of this composition depicts an imaginary creature composed of an Asiatic lion's head, a serpent-like body, a fishtail, and wings. A nude child deity grasps one of the creature's wing with his left hand and holds a short sword in his right hand to control it. A smaller fragment containing the head of a similar composite beast in the British Museum might be the complement to this vignette. The lower right section depicts a nude fertility goddess emerging from vine leaves and grapes. With the increasing influence of Greco-Roman culture during the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE, new artistic styles and motifs, such as this female deity, became part of ancient South Arabian culture.
original_text_note:
THE WALTERS ART MUSEUM'S OWN OBJECT DESCRIPTION, VERBATIM AND ENTIRE. `classify_original` forces `object_description` on any FIND_TYPES record whatever the field contains, and `derive_record_tier` returns `catalogue_record` on the same test, so this is a museum's prose about an object and is not the wording of a primary text.

citation_original:
THE SOURCE NAMES A LICENCE, AND IT IS NOT THE ONE THE OBJECT PAGE ADVERTISES. THE POSITION IS `open_licence_stated` AND THE LICENCE IS THE **GNU FREE DOCUMENTATION LICENSE**.

Quoted verbatim from https://thewalters.org/about/policies/rights-reproductions/, read 2026-09-06:

"Because the Walters owns or has jurisdiction over the objects in its collection and owns or customarily obtains the rights to any imaging of its collection objects, it has adopted the Creative Commons Zero: No Rights Reserved or CC0 license to waive copyright and allow for unrestricted use of digital images and metadata by any person, for any purpose. The longer text descriptions about the artworks on this website are released under the GNU Free Documentation License."

THE SECOND SENTENCE IS THE ONE THAT GOVERNS THIS RECORD. What this record takes is a longer text description about an artwork — 700 characters of curatorial prose — and the same paragraph that grants CC0 over images and metadata assigns that material to a different licence. The object page at art.thewalters.org/object/21.74/ shows eleven `Creative Commons License` badges, every one of them beside a `Download Image` control and every one of them linking to https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/. **A reader of the object page alone would record this record's text as CC0 and would be wrong.** That is FINDING 87.

NO VERSION IS NAMED. The policy says `GNU Free Documentation License` and stops, and the corpus records what is printed rather than levelling it to a version, which is the treatment F6 gave an `open_licence_stated` licence that named no version either.

WHY NOT `two_positions_stated`: the page states two licences over two DIFFERENT bodies of material and says which is which. That is one position per thing, cleanly, and the record knows which thing it took. `two_positions_stated` is for a record whose own material has two positions asserted over it, which `eastasia-08-songshi-fulin` has and this does not.
notes:
F7's Arabia `catalogue_record` slot. Second record of the tranche, forty-ninth in the corpus.

WHY THIS OBJECT AND NOT ANOTHER SOUTH ARABIAN PIECE. The tier needs a museum's own words connecting the region to Rome, and that is the hardest attribute to find in a catalogue: most object records describe an object and stop. This one ends with a sentence that is an argument — "With the increasing influence of Greco-Roman culture during the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE, new artistic styles and motifs, such as this female deity, became part of ancient South Arabian culture." A nude fertility goddess emerging from vine leaves and grapes, on a pediment at Maʾrib, described by the institution that owns it as Greco-Roman influence arriving in South Arabia. The corpus's other Arabian records are inscriptions and a tax tariff; this is the first time it holds Rome reaching Arabia as an IMAGE rather than as a word.

AND IT SITS AT THE SAME PLACE AS THE RECORD CURATED BEFORE IT. `arabia-07-cih541` is the Great Dam inscription at Maʾrib, where the ambassador of the king of Rome arrives at a South Arabian court in 548 CE. This pediment is from the same town four centuries earlier, and what arrives is a motif. Two records, one gazetteer id, two blocks — a findspot and an origin — and two completely different kinds of contact.

NOT DECLARED GLOSS-CAPABLE, AND IT COULD HAVE BEEN. The description contains a hedged identification in the museum's own words, inside the chunked field: "A smaller fragment containing the head of a similar composite beast in the British Museum **might be** the complement to this vignette." That is mechanically what `what_gloss_capable_MEANS_mechanically` asks for. It is not declared because F7 holds ONE declaration, Block F's last, and it is spent on `persia-07-met-ewer-anahita`, whose hedge is a genuine dispute about meaning rather than a suggestion about a join. A second declaration is over-delivery that `check_delivery` fails on the day it happens. Recorded here so that a later block can see the material exists without re-reading the record to find it — the same service `persia-06` and `scandinavia-07` do for F6.

THE PROVENANCE IS MARKET-DERIVED AND IS QUOTED RATHER THAN SUMMARISED. London 1963, Baltimore 1965, gift 2014. South Arabian material is subject to live restitution questions and this record takes no position on them; what it does is publish the chain the museum publishes, so that a reader is never in the position of learning it somewhere else.

SECOND RECORD IN THE CORPUS WITH `source_type` `object_record`, after `persia-07-met-ewer-anahita` an hour earlier.
